title: Run-Length Code Capped at Nine
statement:
Compress a lowercase string word like this. Start with an empty result. While word is not empty, take the longest prefix that is one letter repeated, but at most 9 letters long. Append its length (a single digit) followed by the letter to the result, and remove that prefix from word.

Return the compressed string.

examples.why: Twelve z's do not fit in one digit, so they become a block of 9 and a block of 3.
Single letters still get a count of 1.
Runs are contiguous. The two groups of a's are separate blocks, not one count of 4.

constraints: word has only lowercase English letters
hints: Walk the string once. What do you need to remember about the current block?
Keep the current letter and how many you have seen in a row. When the letter changes, the block ends.
A block also ends when its count reaches 9, even if the same letter continues. Collect the pieces in an array and join once.

explain.intuition:
This is ordinary run-length encoding with one extra rule: a block may not grow past 9. So the block ends in two situations: the next letter is different, or the block already has 9 letters.

Use two pointers: i marks the start of a block and j walks forward while the letter matches and j − i < 9. Emit j − i and the letter, then start the next block at j.
steps: Set i = 0 and an empty list of pieces.
Move j from i while word[j] === word[i] and j − i < 9.
Push String(j − i) + word[i] and set i = j.
Repeat until i reaches the end, then join the pieces.
pitfalls: Writing the real run length (like 12z) instead of splitting into blocks of at most 9.
Building the result with += in a language where strings are immutable and concatenation copies, which can turn the loop quadratic.
Dropping the last block because the loop only emits when the letter changes.

solutions.title: Two pointers per block
solutions.idea: Extend each block while the letter matches and it holds fewer than 9 letters.

solutions.title: Full runs, then split
solutions.idea: Find each maximal run, then emit floor(len / 9) blocks of 9 and one remainder block.

followups: Write the decoder. Why does capping at 9 make decoding easier?
Compress in place in a character array and return the new length. Can the output ever be longer than the input?
